Peter D. Adams PhD: The Adams lab studies how aging cells change at the level of chromatin (the packaging of DNA) and how that drives both cancer and tissue aging. When cells become "senescent" — permanently stopped from dividing, usually after stress or a cancer-causing mutation gets switched on — their epigenome is dramatically reprogrammed. Short-term, this senescence blocks tumors from forming. But senescent cells that build up over a lifetime cause chronic inflammation and aging of tissues, and can even promote tumors. The lab discovered that senescent cells expel fragments of chromatin (called CCF) into the cytoplasm, where they are detected by an antiviral DNA-sensing pathway (cGAS/STING) that triggers inflammation. Understanding this chromatin-to-inflammation pathway could point to interventions for healthy aging and cancer prevention, since aging is the single biggest risk factor for most cancers.
Anindya Bagchi PhD: The Bagchi lab studies the genetic mutations that drive cancer, aiming to find the specific mutations cancer cells depend on to survive — their "Achilles heel." Using genetics-based approaches, the lab has identified and characterized several key mutations that, as a proof of concept, can be targeted in as much as 30% of all cancers. The idea is that if a mutation is truly a cancer's lifeline, blocking it should selectively kill the cancer cells while sparing normal ones. The lab's current focus is extending this proof-of-concept work toward therapies that could eventually be tested in clinical trials, translating basic genetic discoveries into actionable cancer treatments.
Anne Bang PhD: The Bang lab builds lab-grown human disease models using stem cells — including cells reprogrammed from patients (hiPSCs) — mainly to study neurological and neuromuscular disease and to screen for new drugs. They engineer high-throughput assays that measure things like neuron shape, mitochondrial function, and electrical activity, so that complex disease features can be tested at the scale needed for drug discovery. The lab has run large screens on cells from muscular dystrophy patients, heart cells derived from stem cells, and neurons from Alzheimer's patients, uncovering a druggable pathway linking neuronal cholesterol handling to Alzheimer's-related damage. Bang's earlier work also helped develop stem-cell-derived pancreatic cells for diabetes treatment. Overall, the lab pairs stem cell technology with scalable testing to turn basic biology into therapeutic leads.
Rolf Bodmer PhD: The Bodmer lab studies how organs form and function properly, using the fruit fly (Drosophila) as a model to study heart development and aging. By studying the genes that build and maintain the fly heart, the lab aims to uncover basic principles of organ formation that likely apply more broadly. They also study how the HIF and Notch signaling pathways let organisms respond to low oxygen (hypoxia), work that is relevant to cancer since tumors often experience low-oxygen conditions. A separate line of research examines master regulatory networks controlling metabolism and obesity, which is also connected to cancer metabolism. The lab's genetic studies in flies have helped identify new genes linked to heart defects in human patients.
Paul Boutros PhD, MBA: The Boutros lab uses computational and data science tools, including artificial intelligence and machine learning, to understand why cancer develops differently from patient to patient. By analyzing very large datasets of cancer DNA and protein content, the team looks for unexpected patterns that reveal new cancer biology, new drug targets, and new biomarkers for early diagnosis. A recent example is a method to analyze the "dark proteome" — proteins in tumors that standard techniques cannot detect — which the team is now applying in clinical trials studying how exercise affects cancer progression. The lab also builds and shares large datasets and software tools meant to accelerate cancer research broadly, reflecting the idea that each patient's cancer is genetically unique even though cancers share common features.
Linda Bradley PhD: The Bradley lab studies how immune T cells are regulated, particularly how they migrate into tissues and how well they remember past infections, using in vivo (whole-organism) models. Current work centers on two molecules, CD44 and PSGL-1, that guide T cells from the blood into tissue and also independently control how strong and long-lasting a T cell response is. The lab studies both acute virus infections, where T cells successfully clear the virus, and chronic infections, where T cells lose function over time — a process also relevant to cancer, where tumor-fighting T cells become exhausted. Working with UCSD's Moores Cancer Center, the lab pursues translational studies aimed at boosting T cell responses against infections and tumors, and dampening them in autoimmune disease, with an eye toward new biologic therapies.
Lukas Chavez PhD: The Chavez lab focuses on childhood brain cancers, working directly with physicians and scientists to collect genomic, transcriptomic, and epigenetic data from pediatric brain tumor patients to improve diagnosis and treatment. A major research interest is circular extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) and other structural DNA variants found in tumor cells — these DNA circles occur frequently in highly aggressive solid tumors and represent a promising new target for therapies. The lab uses computational and bioinformatic approaches, including gene expression and genomic analysis, to connect these DNA abnormalities to tumor behavior. Their work has also shown that mouse models built from patient tumor samples closely resemble the original human tumors, supporting their use in further research.
Jerold Chun MD, PhD: The Chun lab works on neuroscience drug discovery and on a phenomenon called genomic mosaicism, in which individual brain cells surprisingly carry different DNA sequences from one another. The lab studies what causes this mosaicism, which cell types are affected, and how it relates to diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Down syndrome, and psychiatric disorders. A second major focus is lysophospholipid signaling — small fat molecules like LPA and S1P that act through cell-surface receptors and are involved in conditions such as hydrocephalus, schizophrenia, autism, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's. This receptor research previously contributed to developing fingolimod, the first oral treatment for multiple sclerosis, and continues to inform the search for new brain-disease drug targets and biomarkers.
Alexandre Colas PhD: The Colas lab studies how human heart cells develop, aiming to identify the regulatory pathways that determine cardiovascular cell fate. The team has built high-throughput, cell-based screening assays that let them test many conditions at once to uncover these pathways in an unbiased way. Their goal is to use this knowledge to produce better lab-grown heart muscle cells for modeling cardiac disease "in a dish," to develop regenerative strategies for damaged hearts, and to discover new drugs that promote cardiac regeneration or help preserve heart function after injury, such as after a heart attack. Related work from the lab has also explored gene networks involved in atrial fibrillation and mechanisms of cellular reprogramming.
Cosimo Commisso PhD: The Commisso lab studies macropinocytosis, a process cells use to gulp in large volumes of fluid from their surroundings. The lab discovered that cancer cells with mutated Ras genes — a very common cancer-driving mutation — rely on this process to bring in amino acids like glutamine that fuel their growth, and showed that blocking this nutrient-delivery route can specifically slow Ras-driven tumors. They also developed methods to detect and measure macropinocytosis directly in tumor tissue. Current work focuses on pancreatic cancer, examining how metabolic stress shapes the tumor's environment and looking for new molecular targets whose blockade could starve tumors of nutrients, as well as exploring macropinocytosis as a route for delivering cancer drugs like nanoparticles.
Nicholas Cosford PhD: The Cosford lab develops small-molecule drug compounds that interact with disease-relevant proteins and cell signaling pathways, using medicinal chemistry and chemical biology methods. One focus is on pathways controlling cell survival and growth, studied with the goal of finding new therapies for cancer, central nervous system diseases, and infectious diseases. The lab also develops synthetic chemistry techniques, including microfluidic technology, to make biologically active compounds more quickly. Cosford's earlier industry work at Sibia Neurosciences and Merck included advancing a nicotinic drug candidate for Parkinson's disease into Phase II clinical trials, and his lab continues this drug-discovery approach — from identifying a promising compound to optimizing it as a potential treatment for diseases including Alzheimer's, ALS, and several cancers.
Maximiliano D'Angelo PhD: The D'Angelo lab studies nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) — large multiprotein channels that span the nuclear envelope and control which molecules move in and out of the cell nucleus. Beyond acting as transport gateways, NPCs also help regulate gene expression, chromatin organization, and RNA processing in ways that don't depend on transport itself. The lab has found that cells can reconfigure their NPCs to influence processes like T cell activation, muscle differentiation, and tumor development and spread. A major focus is understanding how alterations in this nuclear transport machinery, long observed in cancer cells, actually contribute to cell transformation and tumor growth — a connection that is still poorly understood. The work matters because NPCs are essential for cell survival and differentiation, making them a potential target for future cancer therapies.
Ani Deshpande PhD: The Deshpande lab studies how chromatin (the packaging of DNA) and epigenetic regulation go wrong in blood cancers, particularly Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). They investigate how normal blood stem cells' ability to self-renew gets hijacked by cancer cells, and how mutations in the proteins that read, write, and erase the 'histone code' drive leukemia. Using mouse models and genome-scale approaches, the lab studies chromosomal translocations — genetic rearrangements first linked to cancer via the Philadelphia chromosome — and how they create fusion genes that drive malignancy. The ultimate goal is to connect these basic mechanisms of chromatin regulation to disease and use that knowledge to design targeted therapeutic screens for AML, uncovering new points where the disease could be treated.
Debanjan Dhar PhD: The Dhar lab studies how the liver communicates with other organs — the immune system, heart, and kidneys — to understand and detect diseases earlier. A central focus is metabolic-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a condition where fat builds up in the liver and leads to chronic inflammation and scarring over time. The lab examines how lifestyle factors like high-calorie diets, heavy alcohol use, and low exercise, combined with genetic predisposition, drive these liver, heart, and kidney changes. By studying the signals the liver sends into the bloodstream that may affect the cardiovascular system, the lab hopes to find biomarkers that catch MASH and liver cancer at an earlier, more treatable stage, and to better understand the liver's role as a hub of inter-organ communication rather than an isolated organ.
Brooke Emerling PhD: The Emerling lab studies the signaling and metabolic pathways that let cancer cells survive and grow. Their main focus is a family of lipid-modifying enzymes called PI5P4Ks (phosphatidylinositol-5-phosphate 4-kinases), studied using human, mouse, and worm models. A major project examines the role of these enzymes in p53-mutant cancers, especially triple-negative breast cancer, a subtype where existing targeted therapies often fail. Related work has shown that these kinases help cancer cells move cholesterol within the cell to fuel growth pathways, and that pancreatic cancer cells rely on specific enzymes to obtain nutrients. The lab's approach combines cancer metabolism and lipid signaling research, aiming to find new metabolic vulnerabilities that could be exploited to 'starve' hard-to-treat tumors.
Shengjie Feng PhD: The Feng lab studies ion channels — proteins that span cell membranes and control the flow of charged particles like sodium, calcium, and potassium in and out of cells — in both healthy and diseased conditions, with a focus on neural cells. These channels are central to how neurons communicate: their coordinated opening and closing generates the electrical signals underlying perception and cognition. Feng uses cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), an imaging technique that uses electron wavelengths to visualize molecules at extremely small scales, along with mouse models, to understand how membrane proteins and ion channels function and malfunction during neural development and disease. This matters because ion channel dysfunction is linked to a wide range of conditions, including epilepsy, muscle tension, diabetes, and various cancers.
Hudson Freeze PhD: The Freeze lab studies glycosylation — the process by which cells attach and sculpt chains of sugar molecules onto proteins and lipids, a process involving over 500 genes that is essential for proteins to fold correctly and function once they reach the cell surface. The lab identifies new glycosylation disorders and investigates how defects in the genes that build, transport, and remodel these sugar chains cause disease, focusing on Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation (CDG), a group of rare inherited conditions. Through collaborations with physicians at medical centers around the US, the lab develops molecular diagnostic methods for CDG patients, studies disease progression, and works toward therapies that could supplement the depleted glycosylation pathways in affected patients — work aimed directly at improving diagnosis and treatment for a historically understudied disease group.
Timothy Huang PhD: The Huang lab studies the molecular mechanisms behind neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, with the goal of identifying neuroprotective pathways that could slow disease progression. Current work centers on two genetic Alzheimer's risk factors, SORLA (SORL1/LR11) and TREM2, which may help protect against the effects of cognitive decline; the lab is exploring whether boosting these protective pathways could help reverse neuronal and cognitive damage. Using techniques including biochemistry, confocal microscopy, electrophysiology, mass spectrometry, and proteomics, the lab studies cell signaling, neuron-glia interactions, and proteolytic pathways involved in neurodegeneration. SORLA in particular is being investigated as a possible drug target for certain types of dementia, connecting basic neuroscience to the search for new Alzheimer's treatments.
Michael Karin PhD: The Karin lab studies how inflammation drives disease, focusing on how metabolism and nutrition affect inflammatory processes, metabolic disorders like type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease (MASLD), and cancers of the pancreas, liver, and gastrointestinal tract. A major line of work traces how liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma) arises from chronic injury and inflammation, including a surprising discovery that cancer-forming progenitor cells emerge from senescent (aged, no-longer-dividing) liver cells rather than being simply suppressed by senescence. The lab also established how immune cytokines and NF-κB signaling pathways, which Karin's group first identified, drive various cancers via both innate and adaptive immune cells. Using mouse models of liver disease, they study how diet, alcohol, and toxicant exposure influence disease progression, helping found the field of Inflammation and Cancer research.
Randal J. Kaufman PhD: The Kaufman lab studies how cells cope with misfolded or unfolded proteins that accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), a process called the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR). The lab has spent over 30 years mapping the three signaling branches of the UPR — IRE1, ATF6, and PERK — which sense protein-folding stress and activate genes to restore normal function or, if damage is too severe, trigger cell death. Notably, they showed that the PERK pathway is essential for insulin production by pancreatic beta cells, linking protein folding directly to blood sugar regulation and diabetes. Their work also explains how cancer cells exploit these same stress pathways to survive hostile conditions, and has implications for other diseases including viral infection, inflammation, and neurodegenerative conditions like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.
Kelly Kersten PhD: The Kersten lab studies why cancer immunotherapy — treatments that harness a patient's own immune system to fight cancer — fails to work for many patients. Their research focuses on how different immune cells interact within tumors, particularly how macrophages and T cells communicate to either support or suppress anti-tumor immunity. Key questions include why T cells become dysfunctional and 'exhausted' inside tumors, how those exhausted T cells reshape the surrounding immune environment, and how macrophages actively shut down T cells' cancer-killing activity. The lab also examines how harsh tumor conditions — low nutrients, low oxygen, and metabolic stress — impair immune cell function. By defining the molecular signals behind these immune cell interactions, the lab aims to design new strategies that make immunotherapy work for more cancer patients.
Caroline Kumsta PhD: The Kumsta lab studies autophagy — the cell's internal recycling process that clears out damaged proteins and components — and how it relates to aging, stress responses, and neurodegeneration, using the roundworm C. elegans and human tissue. As cells age, damaged proteins and other biomolecules accumulate, contributing to cellular decline and raising the risk of age-related diseases including neurodegeneration. The lab studies 'hormetic' stress responses, where small amounts of stress activate protective cellular mechanisms like autophagy, helping cells maintain function over time. By uncovering how these cyto-protective pathways work, the lab aims to identify strategies for preserving cellular health during aging, with the broader goal of extending healthy lifespan and reducing age-related disease as the global population grows older.
Ahmed Mahmoud PhD: The Mahmoud lab studies why the adult mammalian heart cannot regenerate after injury, while lower vertebrates like zebrafish and even newborn mice briefly can. They investigate the transcriptional, epigenetic, and metabolic networks that control heart muscle cells (cardiomyocytes) as they divide, and how the surrounding cardiac microenvironment (including neural and extracellular signals) shapes regeneration. The lab showed that reprogramming cell metabolism can push adult cardiomyocytes to proliferate, regrow blood vessels, and regenerate after cardiac injury. Using genomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and mouse genetics, they also study how adult heart cells re-enter the cell cycle and disassemble their contractile machinery. The long-term goal is to reactivate the heart's natural regenerative ability in adult humans, offering new therapeutic strategies for heart failure, the leading cause of death worldwide.
Jamey Marth PhD: The Marth lab studies glycosylation, the process by which cells attach sugar chains (glycans) to proteins and lipids, and how this shapes health and disease. Because glycan structures are difficult to predict from genes alone, the lab uses whole-organism approaches in mice, including tools like Cre-lox recombination to switch genes on or off in specific tissues and at specific times. This lets them trace how glycan-modified proteins are recognized by glycan-binding receptors (lectins) and how disruptions in these interactions contribute to diseases including colitis, diabetes, autoimmune disease, and sepsis. Their work treats glycan biology like other well-studied pathways such as protein phosphorylation, aiming to uncover previously hidden layers of biological information encoded in sugar chains that could point to new disease mechanisms and treatments.
Jill Mesirov PhD: The Mesirov lab applies machine-learning methods to genomic and molecular data from patient tumors to understand what makes different cancer subtypes biologically distinct. Beyond discovery research, the lab is known for building free, accessible software tools -- including GenePattern, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (with its Molecular Signature Database), and the Integrative Genomics Viewer -- that let researchers worldwide analyze and visualize large genomic datasets without needing advanced programming skills; these tools are used by over a million researchers in 100 countries. The lab's overarching goal is to help build the foundation for precision oncology, where routine tumor sequencing helps doctors choose therapies tailored to a patient's specific cancer subtype. Mesirov also helps guide computational science strategy across the institute and serves on a pediatric tumor board matching children with genome-informed cancer therapies.
José Luis Millán PhD: The Millán lab studies how the body normally mineralizes bones and teeth, and what goes wrong in diseases that cause soft bones (like Hypophosphatasia, HPP) or abnormal calcification of soft tissues, including blood vessels (relevant to chronic kidney disease). Their work centers on an enzyme called TNAP, whose deficiency in HPP lets a mineralization-blocking molecule build up, causing defective bones and teeth. The lab helped develop an enzyme-replacement therapy (asfotase alfa) that was approved in 2015 to treat pediatric HPP, and is now pursuing gene therapy as an alternative treatment with collaborators in Japan. They have also identified the biological changes that drive artery calcification in several genetic diseases and, with chemists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, developed small-molecule drug candidates now in clinical trials to treat soft-tissue calcification.
Karen Ocorr PhD: The Ocorr lab studies the cellular and molecular basis of heart disease using the fruit fly (Drosophila) as a genetic model system, alongside collaborations using human stem-cell-derived heart cells. One project searches for genes involved in Atrial Fibrillation by comparing fly and human heart cell models. Another examines how metabolism contributes to cardiomyopathy, since obesity and metabolic syndrome raise heart disease risk, focusing on a specific metabolic signaling molecule. A third studies how gravity affects heart function, work relevant both to future space travelers and to bedridden or muscle-wasting patients on Earth. The lab pioneered SOHA, a method for measuring heartbeat parameters in small model-organism hearts, and has identified ion channels shared between fly and human hearts that, when mutated, cause arrhythmia in both.
Andrei Osterman PhD: The Osterman lab uses a systems biology approach to map out metabolic and gene-regulatory networks across organisms ranging from bacteria to humans. They combine comparative genomics and other bioinformatic techniques with biochemical and genetic experiments to discover new genes, enzymes, and pathways, focusing especially on metabolism of cofactors, carbohydrates, and amino acids. This work has led to identifying novel bacterial transporters, regulators, and carbohydrate-processing pathways. In infectious disease, the lab searches for new drug targets and helps design anti-infective agents; in cancer, they apply metabolic profiling to find new diagnostic and therapeutic targets. Osterman also co-founded an organization supporting open-source genome annotation and comparative analysis, reflecting the lab's broader commitment to computational tools for exploring metabolic networks and discovering genes.
Elena Pasquale PhD: The Pasquale lab studies Eph receptors and their partner molecules called ephrins, a cell-communication system the lab helped discover. Using biochemistry, mass spectrometry, molecular biology, and animal models, they map how these receptors are chemically switched on and off (via phosphorylation) and identified binding partners and signaling connections, including a role for one receptor in regulating brain synapses. Because Eph receptors are frequently mutated in cancers such as melanoma, lung, colorectal, and head and neck cancers, the lab now focuses heavily on how these mutations change receptor behavior, sometimes shifting it from suppressing tumors to promoting them. Their work aims to clarify how Eph receptor signaling contributes to cancer and neurodegenerative disease, and to develop agents that target these receptors for research and future treatments.
Pier Lorenzo Puri MD: The Puri lab studies how genes are switched on and off (epigenetics) to control the formation and health of skeletal muscle, using human stem cells and mouse models. They discovered why human embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells normally resist being converted into muscle cells, tracing it to a missing component of a chromatin-remodeling complex, and used this insight to build 3D lab-grown contractile muscle tissue for studying muscle disease such as muscular dystrophy. The lab has also identified transcription factors that activate muscle-specific genes, shown how aging cells become resistant to muscle gene activation due to DNA damage responses, and mapped how a key muscle regulator (MYOD) reorganizes the 3D structure of DNA in the nucleus to turn on muscle genes. Their broader focus includes the many cell types that support muscle health and repair.
Sanjeev S. Ranade PhD: The Ranade lab studies why some children are born with heart defects, a condition affecting nearly 1 in 100 children and linked to earlier-onset heart disease later in life. Building on doctoral training in ion channels (proteins that let charged molecules cross cell membranes and enable cell signaling and muscle contraction) and postdoctoral work connecting genetics to cell biology in heart development, Ranade focuses on transcription factors, proteins that turn genes on and off, and how mutations in them disrupt cell-to-cell signaling needed for normal heart formation. The lab has used CRISPR technology to identify a protein whose overabundance is linked to Down syndrome and congenital heart disease, aiming to uncover the basic rules that govern heart development and what happens when those rules break down.
Alessandra Sacco PhD: The Sacco lab studies muscle stem cells and how they are regulated in the body, with the goal of understanding and eventually treating skeletal muscle wasting, a serious problem in conditions like muscular dystrophy, aging, and HIV that currently has no cure. Muscle stem cells hold promise for future therapies, but the lab notes that this potential is limited by an incomplete understanding of what controls their behavior. Their research examines both external (extrinsic) and internal (intrinsic) factors that regulate these stem cells in living tissue. Prior work from the lab's founder helped establish methods to isolate adult muscle stem cells and provided direct evidence that they can self-renew in the body, and identified a protein (tenascin-C) linked to muscle stem cell levels and regeneration.
Douglas Sheffler PhD: The Sheffler lab studies G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), a large class of proteins that relay signals into cells, focusing on how they bind molecules, get switched off (desensitized), and are internalized or degraded. Much of the lab's work involves discovering and characterizing drug-like molecules that turn specific GPCRs up or down, including muscarinic and glutamate receptor modulators, with applications in schizophrenia and other brain disorders. The lab also studies addiction, including nicotine addiction, and has worked on a compound (SBP-9330) whose mechanism may also apply to cocaine, opioid, and methamphetamine addiction. Combining pharmacology, cell biology, and high-throughput screening, the lab's research has produced more than 45 publications and several patent applications for small-molecule therapeutics targeting neurological and psychiatric conditions.
Sanju Sinha PhD: The Sinha lab uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to develop cancer-preventive therapies, with a particular focus on how aging increases cancer risk, a factor the lab says is often overlooked. They analyze multi-omics data (multiple types of large-scale biological data) to understand how aging changes the tissue environment in ways that raise cancer susceptibility, then use those insights to design preventive drug candidates targeting those specific changes. The lab has built computational tools including a single-cell-based framework for predicting patient treatment response and drug resistance in precision oncology, and DeepTarget, a tool that integrates genetic and drug screening data to figure out how cancer drugs work and what their primary and secondary targets are. They have also studied cancer-related risks associated with CRISPR gene-editing.
Evan Snyder MD, PhD: The Snyder Lab studies stem cell biology, especially neural stem cells (NSCs) — cells that can self-renew and turn into neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. These properties make NSCs promising tools for repairing damage from injury or disease, but the same flexibility also makes them prone to turning cancerous. The lab takes a multidisciplinary approach, studying the basic biology of stem cells, their roles across an individual's lifetime, and their therapeutic potential, aiming to understand normal development, how tissues maintain themselves, and how the body recovers from injury. Their work spans many disease areas, including neurodegenerative conditions, cancer, and spinal cord injury. Research so far has been done in animal models, with the ultimate goal of moving findings into clinical trials. The lab is directed by Dr. Evan Snyder, founding director of the Institute's Stem Cell Research Center.
Charles Spruck PhD: The Spruck lab works on developing new, non-toxic treatments for advanced, metastatic cancers, focusing on breast, lung, prostate, and brain tumors. One major thread studies the molecular pathways that let cancer cells move, invade, and spread (metastasize); the lab identified a pathway (FBXO7/EYA2-SCF(FBXW7)) that drives this spread and found that blocking it reduced metastasis and boosted anti-tumor immune responses in mouse models. A second thread explores "viral mimicry": activating dormant virus-like elements embedded in the genome (endogenous retroviruses and retrotransposons) to make cancer cells more visible to the immune system, enhancing the effectiveness of immunotherapy and DNA-damaging treatments. The lab discovered a gene pathway (FBXO44/SUV39H1) that normally keeps these elements silenced, and disabling it increased tumor immunogenicity. The lab uses biochemistry, CRISPR gene editing, and animal cancer models.
Xueqin (Sherine) Sun PhD: The Sun lab studies how gene expression is controlled — both through changes to DNA sequence (genetic) and changes that affect how DNA is read without altering the sequence itself (epigenetic) — and how errors in this control contribute to cancer, aging, and developmental disorders. The lab's overarching goal is to identify the genetic and epigenetic changes that drive normal cells to become cancerous, understand how developmental and aging processes influence cancer's progression, and pinpoint the specific vulnerabilities these changes create in cancer cells, which could be targeted by future therapies. The lab uses a wide range of techniques, including imaging, genomics, proteomics, and gene editing, across models such as mice, human and mouse cell lines, and stem cells, with particular relevance to brain cancer, leukemia/lymphoma, and other diseases tied to immune and nervous system function.
Kevin Tharp PhD: The Tharp lab studies how cancer cells' metabolism (how they produce and use energy inside mitochondria) is shaped by the physical properties of the tumor microenvironment — the tissue and structures surrounding a tumor. Using genetically engineered mouse models and bioengineered human tumor models, the lab aims to define the mitochondrial changes that are unique to cancer cells growing within tumors. The ultimate goal is to develop new therapies that block the metabolic adaptations cancer cells rely on to metastasize (spread to other parts of the body), which is a major cause of cancer deaths. The lab's work touches on related areas such as the extracellular matrix, cell adhesion, and inflammation, and connects to tissues including adipose (fat) tissue, the mammary gland, and the vasculature.
Xiao Tian PhD: The Tian lab studies the fundamental mechanisms of aging and how they contribute to age-related diseases like cancer and neurodegeneration. Their research suggests that a progressive loss of "epigenetic information" — the chemical marks that control how genes are turned on and off — is a key driver of aging, and the lab investigates how this system is set up, maintained, and why it eventually fails. One notable finding: the lab identified a molecule (high-molecular-mass hyaluronan) that helps explain why naked mole rats resist cancer and live unusually long, and showed this protective mechanism could be transferred to other species. The lab also studies epigenetic reprogramming — restoring lost epigenetic information — as a strategy to reverse aspects of aging, including in disease models like glaucoma. The ultimate goal is to develop safe, effective rejuvenation strategies.
Alessandro Vasciaveo PhD: The Vasciaveo lab uses large-scale datasets — including single-cell biology data — and advanced machine learning to understand how cells communicate and function in both healthy and diseased states, with the goal of identifying key molecular drivers of disease that could serve as precise treatment targets. A major focus is cancer: the lab develops machine learning models to analyze single-cell data and regulatory/signaling networks in order to understand therapy resistance, a major challenge in oncology, and to computationally identify drug compounds and targets capable of disrupting the molecular programs that drive aggressive cancers, including those driven by the MYC gene. The lab's aim is to translate these computational insights into more precise, patient-tailored cancer therapies, building on techniques for reverse-engineering gene regulatory networks.
Kristiina Vuori MD, PhD: The Vuori lab studies the cellular mechanisms behind cancer metastasis — the spread of cancer to other parts of the body, which is responsible for nearly all cancer deaths. Normally, cells depend on staying attached to surrounding tissue and the extracellular matrix to survive; if a cell detaches, it dies through a process called apoptosis, which is a safeguard that keeps tissues healthy and prevents cells from becoming cancerous. Cancer cells somehow escape this rule, allowing them to break away from a tumor, travel through the body, and establish new tumors elsewhere without dying. Dr. Vuori's research aims to identify the molecular mechanisms that make normal cells dependent on this attachment for survival, with the idea that faulty versions of these same mechanisms are what let cancer cells metastasize — pointing toward ways to block that process.
Eric Wang PhD: The Wang lab focuses on transcriptional regulators — proteins that control which genes are turned on or off — which are commonly disrupted in both tumor cells and the immune cells surrounding them in cancer. The lab develops and uses chemical tools to modulate the activity of these key regulators, with the long-term goal of finding new therapeutic approaches. Eric Wang's background is in chemical biology, with specific expertise in kinase inhibitors and targeted protein degradation — an approach where small molecules recruit the cell's own protein-disposal machinery (E3 ligase complexes) to tag disease-driving proteins for destruction. He also has experience using drugs to adjust immune cell activity in order to improve the immune system's ability to fight tumors (anti-tumor immunity).
Yu Xin (Will) Wang PhD: The Wang lab studies how different cell types work together to repair tissue after injury, with a particular focus on tissue-specific stem cells and how the immune system shapes regeneration versus how autoimmunity can interfere with it. The lab combines molecular, genetic, computational (including machine learning), and bioengineering approaches, using multi-omics sequencing and imaging to trace these processes. A specific aim is understanding the crosstalk between muscle, nerve, and immune systems in order to design targeted therapies for autoimmune neuromuscular disorders and for "inflammaging" — inflammation associated with aging. The lab's research grew out of earlier work on how muscle stem cells self-renew and regenerate skeletal muscle, and is relevant to conditions such as muscular dystrophy, ALS, and age-related muscle loss (sarcopenia).
Yu Yamaguchi MD, PhD: The Yamaguchi lab studies proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans — sugar-containing molecules involved in development — and what happens when the body can't make them properly. The lab creates mutant mice that lack specific glycosaminoglycans (such as heparan sulfate and hyaluronan) to study their roles, and uses this approach to investigate two human disorders: multiple hereditary exostoses (MHE), a bone disease causing abnormal growths, and autism. By selectively removing the Ext1 gene (needed to build heparan sulfate) in specific tissues, the lab has shown that heparan sulfate is important for brain development and bone/joint formation, and built a mouse model that finally reproduces MHE's bony-growth symptoms — revealing that these growths are made of both mutant and normal bone cells. The lab's broader goal is to use these models to test potential drugs for MHE and related disorders.
Yuk-Lap (Kevin) Yip PhD: The Yip lab studies how genes are turned on and off (gene regulatory mechanisms) using computational modeling rather than traditional wet-lab experiments. The lab develops new methods for analyzing large biological datasets, including those from cutting-edge technologies like single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and builds computational models that predict how disruptions to gene regulation affect cells — generating testable hypotheses for studying human diseases such as cancer, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disease. Dr. Yip's research over nearly 20 years has centered on three areas: building computational tools for new experimental data types, studying gene regulation using machine learning, and interpreting genomic and epigenomic changes found in disease. He also leads the Institute's Center for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence.
Su-Chun Zhang MD, PhD: The Zhang lab studies how the many specialized types of neurons and glial cells that make up the human brain are formed, both during development and in efforts to repair a damaged or diseased brain. The lab has developed methods to guide human stem cells (embryonic and induced pluripotent stem cells) into specific, functional nerve cell types, and showed that when transplanted into animal brains, these stem-cell-derived neurons can grow to the correct regions, connect to the right targets, and receive appropriate signals — mimicking normal brain development. The lab is testing the therapeutic potential of these transplanted neurons in animal models (including non-human primates) of Parkinson's disease, stroke, and spinal cord injury, and is preparing for a clinical trial of cell therapy for Parkinson's disease. The lab also studies motor neuron diseases (ALS, SMA), Alzheimer's, and Down syndrome, and builds stem-cell-based models for drug discovery.
Jianhua Zhao PhD: The Zhao lab studies how proteins work, and how that changes in disease, by looking at their physical shape and structure. Dr. Zhao specializes in cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a technique that flash-freezes protein samples and images them to reveal their three-dimensional structure at high resolution. Understanding a protein's precise shape helps explain how it normally functions and what goes wrong when disease occurs, which can point toward new therapeutic targets. Dr. Zhao's own training spans this kind of structural work: his PhD research examined rotary ATPases (molecular motors that help cells manage energy), and his postdoctoral work at UCSF focused on Transient Receptor Potential ion channels, proteins involved in sensing signals like temperature and pressure.
